1EasyCounterexample

True or false, with proof: the continuous image of an open interval is always an open set.

f(x)=x2,I=(−1,1),f(I)=[0,1)f(x) = x^2, \qquad I = (-1, 1), \qquad f(I) = [0, 1)f(x)=x2,I=(−1,1),f(I)=[0,1)
Verdict

The claim is false — the image of the open interval I=(−1,1)I = (-1, 1)I=(−1,1) under f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 is [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1), which is not an open set.

Show solution

Counterexample and verification

  1. False. f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 on R\mathbb{R}R is continuous and I=(−1,1)I = (-1, 1)I=(−1,1) is an open interval. We claim f(I)=[0,1)f(I) = [0, 1)f(I)=[0,1).

    If 0≤y<10 \le y < 10≤y<1 then x=y∈[0,1)⊂Ix = \sqrt{y} \in [0, 1) \subset Ix=y​∈[0,1)⊂I and f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y, so y∈f(I)y \in f(I)y∈f(I). If y<0y < 0y<0 it is unreachable since x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0; if y≥1y \ge 1y≥1 it is unreachable since ∣x∣<1|x| < 1∣x∣<1 implies x2<1x^2 < 1x2<1.

  2. [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1) is not open in R\mathbb{R}R: 0∈[0,1)0 \in [0, 1)0∈[0,1) but for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, −ε/2∈(−ε,ε)-\varepsilon/2 \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)−ε/2∈(−ε,ε) while −ε/2∉[0,1)-\varepsilon/2 \notin [0, 1)−ε/2∈/[0,1).

    So the continuous image [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1) of the open interval is not open. Continuity does not preserve openness (it does preserve closedness via compactness: the continuous image of a compact set is compact).
